com: Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen. Idolatrous Rome is fallen. That mighty seat of power and dominion is fallen. The long fixed abode of voluptuousness and luxury, for the merchants of the earth have become rich by the strength of her delicacies, and now the hand of God hath struck her. It is utterly destroyed; not a human being in it. Thus it is become an accursed place, given up for an habitation of devils and a hold of every unclean spirit, or of frightful spectres and ghosts, and a hold of every unclean and hateful bird, of owls, ravens, vultures, &c. &c. (Pastorini)

Go out from her, my people. The people of God, the Christians, are all here told to leave the falling city, lest they be partakers of her sins, and receive of her plagues. At the time of Alaric’s sacking Rome, many fled away to St. Jerome, who was then in Judea; others fled into other parts, as many holy fathers testify. St. Jerome says, (Ep. vii) that St. Paula and several illustrious Christian families had left Rome as if by particular inspiration, and retired into Judea. The holy pope Innocent was drawn by a particular providence out of the city, as Lot out of Sodom, that he might not see the ruin of a guilty people, says Orosius, lib. 7. chap. xxxix. We read likewise that Melania, as if she foresaw the approaching catastrophe, had prevailed upon many Christians to retire with her from a city doomed to destruction. (Histor. Laus. chap. cxviii.) In fine, we all know that when the storm broke out, the Christians took refuge and were saved in the Churches of St. Peter and St. Paul, which Alaric had allowed to be places of safety. (Haydock)
Alas! alas! St. Augustine informs us, that the people of the eastern provinces, and the remotest cities, mourned in a public manner on this occasion. (De Civ. Dei. lib. 1, chap. xxxiii.)

We see here enumerated the articles of the luxury of the pagan Romans in dress, in ornaments, in furniture, in equipage, in the sumptuousness of their tables, &c. &c. Nothing is more remarkable than the extravagant luxury and profusion of some of the Roman emperors at their tables. Caligula once spent (according to Seneca) for a supper, 150,000 crowns. Suetonius tells us, that the emperor Vitellius would feast himself thrice, and often four times in a day, spending 10,000 crowns at each meal. But now they are all gone; they are now the fuel of fire, and in one hour brought to nought. (Haydock)

Rejoice….heaven, the holy apostles and prophets, and all the holy ministers of the gospel: and holy men are invited here to rejoice, because the divine justice is accomplished in the ruin of that guilty city. (Pastorini) — By the words prophets, &c. are not meant those of the old law, as pagan Rome had not been the cause of their deaths, but here only includes all the prophets, saints, and martyrs, who had been put to death for Christ throughout the whole Roman empire. (Haydock)
fa: Commentary on Revelation

After these things I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great power, and the earth was illuminated by his glory. The things that follow refer in general to the ungodly city, that is, to all the wicked. And in order to show more fully the overthrow of Babylon, he returns to its first ruin, by which it was overthrown through Christ. For this angel signifies Christ, who consented to come down from heaven to earth, so that he might lift humans up to heavenly things. He is said to have great power because he has the same power as the Father, since in all things he is equal to the Father. …
On the Resurrection of the Flesh

No one has as yet fallen in with Elias; no one has as yet escaped from Antichrist; no one has as yet had to bewail the downfall of Babylon. And is there now anybody who has risen again, except the heretic? He, of course, has already quitted the grave of his own corpse-although he is even now liable to fevers and ulcers; he, too, has already trodden down his enemies-although he has even now to struggle with the powers of the world.
Commentary on Revelation
And he cried out in a loud voice, saying: The voice of Christ is the teaching of the Gospel. But what this voice cried out he makes clear by adding:
Commentary on Revelation

Babylon the great has fallen, has fallen. To have said something, for God, is to have done it; for he said that Babylon had fallen, because he himself brought about its fall. It is said to have fallen twice, because it fell the first time when, through the teaching of the Gospel, it lost a very great multitude of the elect, who, cut off from it through faith in Christ, became citizens of the holy city, that is, of the Church. It will fall a second time, when on the last day it will be punished with everlasting death, which in this book is called the second death.
Commentary on Revelation

And it became a dwelling place of demons. Were demons not dwelling in Babylon before the coming of Christ? They certainly were, but their dwelling was unknown. However, when the multitude of the elect was converted to the faith, Babylon became known as the dwelling place of demons, because those who accepted the faith of Christ truly came to know that the dwelling of demons had always been in Babylon.
Commentary on Revelation

Because all the nations have drunk of the wine of her wrath, and the kings of the earth have committed fornication with her, and the merchants of the earth have become rich by the power of her luxuries. What the wine of wrath is, and what the fornication of the kings with Babylon is, however, we have briefly said above. By the merchants of the earth we can understand the lovers of this world, who hand over their souls to destruction for the gaining of money. Of merchants of this sort Jesus, son of Sirach, speaks, saying: For this man has made his soul for sale; for in his lifetime he cast forth his innermost being (Sirach 10:10). …
Letters
Letter 46

… here he was wrapped in swaddling clothes; here he was seen by the shepherds; here he was pointed out by the star; here he was adored by the wise men.… Read the Apocalypse of John, and consider what is sung therein of the woman arrayed in purple and of the blasphemy written upon her brow.… "Come out of her, my people," so the Lord says, "that you be not partakers of her sins and that you receive not of her plagues." … It is true that Rome has a holy church, trophies of apostles and martyrs, a true confession of Christ. …
Treatise 12. Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews
Treatise XII Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews

That the believer ought not to live like the Gentile. In Jeremiah: "Thus saith the Lord, Walk ye not according to the way of the Gentiles. Of this same thing, that one ought to separate himself from the Gentiles, lest he should be a companion of their sin, and become a partaker of their penalty, in the Apocalypse: "And I heard another voice from heaven, saying, Go forth from her, my people, lest thou be partaker of her crimes, and lest thou be stricken with her plagues; because her crimes have reached even to heaven, and the Lord God hath remembered her iniquities. …
The Chaplet, or De Corona
De Corona
From so much as a dwelling in that Babylon of John's Revelation we are called away; much more then from its pomp.
Commentary on Revelation

And I heard another voice from heaven saying. By heaven in this place the Church is signified; the voice from heaven is the voice of preachers proceeding from the Church. But what does this voice say?
Commentary on Revelation

Go out from her, my people. Through his preachers the Lord urges the elect to go out from Babylon, not in body, but in mind. How, however, they ought to go out from Babylon he teaches in what follows, saying:
Commentary on Revelation

For her sins have reached all the way to heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities. The Almighty God always beholds the iniquities of Babylon; but when He does not exact vengeance, He appears not to see what He sees. By this, therefore, what he says points to that time in which all the wicked will be punished with eternal torment.
Commentary on Revelation

Render to her as she herself has rendered to you. The chosen are commanded to repay Babylon as she has repaid them, either because the saints of God will judge the wicked, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “In the renewal of all things, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28); or because they themselves are members of him to whom the power of judging has been handed over by the Father. …
Commentary on Revelation

And repay her double, twice over, according to her works. Babylon persecuted God’s chosen in a twofold way, when she inflicted many evils on their bodies and on their souls. She herself will receive punishments in a twofold way, because bodies will be tormented together with souls; and her “double” will itself be doubled, because for the temporal and brief punishments with which she afflicted the righteous, she will receive eternal punishments.
Commentary on Revelation
In the cup that she mixed for you, mix for her double. By the cup we can understand the tribulations that the saints suffered from the wicked.
Commentary on Revelation

As much as she has glorified herself and lived in luxury, give her that much torment and sorrow. As much as she has glorified herself, that is, raised herself up in pride and entangled herself in every vice, by that much she will also receive greater torments.
Commentary on Revelation

For she says in her heart: “I sit as queen, I am no widow, and I shall not see mourning.” Babylon in a certain way calls herself queen when she exalts herself in the prosperity of this world. She says she is not a widow, because she is joined to temporal goods and nourishes her own luxury from them, and trusts that she cannot be separated from them. She says she will not see mourning, because the wicked, although they know that they are to be punished for their crimes, pretend not to see what they see, and drive the memory of death from their mind, so that sorrowful reflection may not disturb the joy of their heart.
Commentary on Revelation

Therefore in one day her plagues will come: death, and mourning, and famine. On the day of judgment, everlasting death will come upon her, which in this book is called the second death. Mourning will come upon her, as the Lord says in the Gospel: There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. 8:12). Famine will come upon her, that is, the famine of rest; for they will long to find rest from the punishments they endure, but they will by no means attain to that rest.
Commentary on Revelation
And it will be burned with fire; That is, with eternal fire.
Commentary on Revelation

For the Lord is mighty, who will judge her. And the kings of the earth who committed fornication with her and lived in luxury with her will weep and mourn over her when they see the smoke of her burning, standing far off because of fear of her torments, saying: “Alas, alas, that city Babylon, that mighty city; for in one hour your judgment has come!” What the fornication of the kings with Babylon is, we explained above; (Rev. 17:2) but it is very strange that they are said to stand far off, when they themselves are to be plunged into the same punishments as the other wicked, who are signified through Babylon. …
Commentary on Revelation

And the merchants of the earth will weep and mourn over her, because no one will buy their merchandise any more. Since above we said that by the merchants of the earth are meant the lovers of this world, (Rev. 18:3) in this place we can understand by merchants those who sell the good that they seem to do. For there are many to whom knowledge of secular laws has been given, who carry the cases of the poor in courts of law; but because they do this not out of love for God, but for the reception of rewards, they do not receive payment from God. …
Commentary on Revelation

The merchandise of gold, and silver, and precious stone, and pearl, and fine linen, and purple, and silk, and scarlet, and every kind of thyine wood, and all vessels of ivory, and all vessels of precious stone, and of bronze, and of iron, and of marble, and cinnamon, and perfumes, and ointment, and incense, and wine, and oil, and fine flour, and wheat, and beasts of burden, and sheep, and horses, and chariots, and slaves, and human souls: and your fruits, the desires of your soul, have departed from you, and all things rich and splendid have perished from you, and merchants of these things will find them no more. …
Commentary on Revelation

Those who have become rich will stand far away from her because of fear of her torments, weeping and mourning, and saying: “Alas, alas, that great city, that was clothed in fine linen and purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and precious stone and pearls; for in one hour such great riches have been brought to nothing!” That the rich of Babylon are said to stand far away is to be understood according to the sense given above, which we explained about the kings.
Commentary on Revelation

And every shipmaster and all who sail on the lake, and the sailors who work on the sea, stood far off and cried out when they saw the place of her burning, saying: “What city is like this great city? And they cast dust on their heads, weeping and mourning, and saying: “Alas, alas, that great city, in which all who have ships on the sea became rich by her prices; for in a single hour she has been laid waste!” …
Commentary on Revelation

These people are also said to have cast ashes on their heads; for often the mind is signified by the head, and sins by ashes. Therefore they will place ashes upon their heads, because the memory of sins will never depart from their minds.
Commentary on Revelation

Rejoice over her, heaven, and holy apostles and prophets; for God has carried out your judgment on her. By “heaven” we can understand the angels; by “apostles,” the fathers of the New Testament; and by “prophets,” the fathers of the Old Testament. They will therefore rejoice when every band of the wicked has been destroyed together with the demons themselves, the authors of iniquities. They will also rejoice because then all wickedness will come to an end, and everlasting justice will be brought forth.
Commentary on Revelation

And one mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone and cast it into the sea, saying: With this violence shall great Babylon be thrown down, and shall be found no more. This angel signifies Christ, who is said to be mighty, because the human mind cannot comprehend how great the strength of Christ is. By the great millstone every multitude of the wicked is represented; and the sea signifies hell [infernum], into which all the wicked will be plunged. Therefore the angel cast the millstone into the sea, because our Lord Jesus Christ, on the day of judgment, by his just judgment will plunge the whole multitude of the wicked into hell [infernum].
Commentary on Revelation

And every craftsman, and every skill will no longer be found in you, and the sound of the mill will no longer be heard in you, and the light of the lamp will no longer shine in you, and the voice of bridegroom and bride will no longer be heard in you anymore. We must ask why it counts crafts, and the sound of the mill, and the light of the lamp, and the voice of bridegroom and bride among the crimes of Babylon; since all these things can be practiced without guilt, and without them human life cannot exist. Therefore all these things must be understood spiritually. …
Commentary on Revelation
And the sound of harpists, and musicians, and flute players and trumpets will no longer be heard in you. This was mentioned above.
Commentary on Revelation

For your merchants were the princes of the earth. The Church has her merchants, and Babylon has hers: the merchants of the Church store up their treasures in heaven, where thieves do not dig through and do not steal (Matt. 6:19); but the merchants of Babylon store up their treasures on earth, where thieves dig through and steal.
Commentary on Revelation
And in your sorceries all nations went astray. The sorceries of Babylon are the various errors by which humanity has been deceived.
Commentary on Revelation

And in it was found the blood of the prophets and of the saints, and of all who were slain upon the earth. The blood of the saints was found in it, that is, the crime of the killing of the saints, just as the Lord says to the wicked Jews, with the understanding of all the wicked: “All the righteous blood that has been shed upon the earth shall come upon you” (Matt. 23:35).
ftr: John Litteral, released into the public domain
Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 2, vol. 6 (1893)
